body:
Why do we need food?

Food provides the body with energy and the materials needed for growth, repair and maintenance. Even during sleep, the body uses energy to maintain breathing, circulation, body temperature and other essential functions. Growing children need additional materials to build new tissues.

A meal may contain roti or rice, dal, vegetables and curd. These foods are different because their nutritional contributions are different. Roti and rice provide substantial amounts of carbohydrate, dal contributes protein, vegetables supply vitamins and minerals, and curd provides protein and calcium. Together, they can supply a wider range of nutrients than a meal consisting of only one food.

Nutrition

Nutrition is the process by which an organism obtains food and uses its components for energy, growth, repair and maintenance. A nutrient is a component of food needed for these functions.

Major nutrient groups

At the school level, the 5 major groups of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. Dietary fibre and water are also essential components of a healthy diet.

Macronutrients and micronutrients

Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are called macronutrients because the body generally requires them in relatively large quantities. Vitamins and minerals are called micronutrients because they are needed in much smaller quantities. Small quantity does not mean small importance: a prolonged shortage of a vitamin or mineral can cause a serious deficiency disorder.

  • Carbohydrates: the body's major dietary source of energy.
  • Fats: a concentrated source of energy; also important for cell structure and the absorption of certain vitamins.
  • Proteins: essential for growth, tissue repair and the formation of many enzymes and other body substances.
  • Vitamins: required for normal functions such as vision, blood formation, bone health and blood clotting.
  • Minerals: required for functions such as bone formation, oxygen transport and thyroid hormone production.

Dietary fibre and water

Dietary fibre, also called roughage, is found mainly in plant foods such as whole grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds. Most dietary fibre is not digested by human digestive enzymes. It helps maintain normal bowel movements and supports digestive health. Although some fibre is broken down by intestinal microorganisms, fibre is not classified as a major energy-giving nutrient in the school-level grouping.

Water is essential for transporting substances, regulating body temperature, supporting digestion and absorption, and removing wastes through urine and sweat. Water is obtained from drinks as well as moisture present in foods such as fruits, vegetables and cooked dishes.

One food can contain several nutrients

Food groups describe what a food is particularly rich in; they do not mean that the food contains only one nutrient. For example, groundnuts contain both fats and proteins. Milk contains water, protein, fat, carbohydrate and calcium. Pulses provide protein along with carbohydrate, fibre and minerals.

Important distinction: A food described as protein-rich or carbohydrate-rich may contain several other nutrients. Likewise, consuming sufficient calories does not necessarily mean that the diet provides sufficient vitamins and minerals.

Prelims focus

  • The 5 major nutrient groups are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals.
  • Carbohydrates and fats mainly provide energy; proteins are essential for growth and repair.
  • Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients required in small quantities.
  • Dietary fibre and water are essential components of a balanced diet.
  • Trap: A food rich in one nutrient is not necessarily a source of only that nutrient.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 8–16, copy marked 2018–19; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body, printed pp. 39–47; ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, Guideline 1, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A varied meal supplies different nutrients needed for health and growth.

title: Nutrition and the Essential Components of Food

body:
Carbohydrates: the main dietary energy source

Carbohydrates provide energy for physical activity and normal body functions. Common dietary carbohydrates include sugars and starch. Sugars are relatively simple carbohydrates, while starch is a complex carbohydrate that the digestive system breaks down into simpler sugars before absorption.

Important carbohydrate sources in Indian diets include rice, wheat, maize, bajra, jowar, potatoes and sweet potatoes. Fruits, milk and pulses also supply carbohydrates. The amount and type differ among foods.

Whole grains and millets are useful because they can supply carbohydrate together with dietary fibre and other nutrients. Refined sugar supplies energy but little protein, fibre or micronutrients. Therefore, a high-energy food is not necessarily a nutritionally balanced food.

Fats: concentrated energy and other functions

Fats provide more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins. They help form cell structures, supply essential fatty acids and enable the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Food sources include groundnuts, sesame seeds, other nuts and seeds, edible oils, ghee, butter, milk products, eggs and fish. The fat content varies considerably among these foods.

Dietary fats are necessary, but excessive consumption of high-fat, energy-dense foods can contribute to excess calorie intake and unhealthy weight gain. Unsaturated fats from nuts, seeds and suitable vegetable oils are generally preferable to frequent consumption of foods rich in saturated fats or industrial trans fats.

Proteins: growth, repair and body functions

Proteins are made from smaller units called amino acids. The body uses amino acids to build and repair tissues and to make many enzymes, hormones and other substances. Proteins can also provide energy, but their role is not limited to energy production.

Important plant sources include moong, tuvar dal, chana, rajma, peas, soybean and groundnuts. Animal sources include milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish and meat.

Cereals and pulses often complement each other nutritionally because their protein compositions differ. Eating wheat or rice with adequate dal, beans or other protein-rich foods helps improve the overall protein quality of the meal. This does not mean that every cereal-and-pulse combination is automatically a complete balanced diet.

Comparing energy values

Food energy is commonly expressed in kilocalories, abbreviated as kcal. The approximate energy provided by 1 g of each macronutrient is:

Thus, 1 g of fat provides approximately 9 kcal, while 1 g of carbohydrate or protein provides approximately 4 kcal. This is an energy comparison, not a ranking of which nutrient is healthiest.

Typical food-source comparisons

NutrientCommon sourcesMain nutritional contribution
CarbohydrateRice, wheat, bajra, maize, potatoEnergy
ProteinDal, soybean, chana, milk, eggsGrowth and tissue repair
FatGroundnut, sesame, nuts, oils, gheeConcentrated energy and essential fatty acids

Remember: Carbohydrates and fats mainly supply energy, but proteins are also energy-yielding nutrients. The phrase body-building foods highlights the important structural functions of proteins; it does not mean proteins are the only nutrients needed for growth.

Prelims focus

  • Starch and sugars are carbohydrates.
  • Rice, wheat, bajra and potatoes are familiar carbohydrate-rich foods.
  • Dal, soybean, chana, milk and eggs are important protein sources.
  • Groundnuts and sesame seeds can supply both fats and proteins.
  • Approximate energy values: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4 kcal/g and fat 9 kcal/g.
  • Trap: More calories per gram does not make fat a nutritionally complete food.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 9–14; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body, printed pp. 39–42; ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, Guidelines 1, 7 and 8; FSSAI, guidance on balanced diets and dietary energy, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: For equal masses of 1 g, carbohydrate and protein each supply approximately 4 kcal, while fat supplies 9 kcal; this compares energy density only.
pictures.caption: Equal weights of fat provide more energy than carbohydrate or protein.

title: Carbohydrates, Proteins and Fats: Functions and Food Sources

body:
What are vitamins?

Vitamins are organic nutrients required in small quantities for normal growth and body functions. They do not directly supply significant dietary energy. Different vitamins perform different functions, so an adequate amount of one vitamin cannot compensate for a deficiency of another.

A prolonged shortage of a particular vitamin may produce a characteristic deficiency disease. The effects depend on the vitamin, the severity and duration of deficiency, and the person's health and dietary condition.

Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins

Vitamins are classified according to how they dissolve. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. They are absorbed with dietary fats and can be stored in the body to varying degrees. Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins are water-soluble. Most water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts, although vitamin B12 is an important exception because substantial stores may be maintained in the liver.

Important vitamin-deficiency associations

VitaminMain functionUseful food sourcesDeficiency association
ANormal vision and epithelial healthCarrot, papaya, mango, green leafy vegetables, milkNight blindness; severe deficiency may damage the eyes
B1 (thiamine)Energy metabolism and nerve functionWhole grains, pulses, seeds, nutsBeriberi
B3 (niacin)Normal energy metabolismGroundnuts, whole grains, legumes, fishPellagra
B9 (folate)Cell division and red blood cell formationGreen leafy vegetables, pulsesMegaloblastic anaemia
B12 (cobalamin)Red blood cell formation and nerve healthAnimal-source foods and fortified foodsMegaloblastic anaemia; neurological problems
CCollagen formation and wound healingAmla, guava, citrus fruits, green chilliScurvy
DCalcium absorption and bone healthFish, eggs, fortified foods; also formed in skin with sunlightRickets in children; osteomalacia in adults
KNormal blood clottingGreen leafy vegetables and other foodsBleeding tendency in severe deficiency

Understanding the classical deficiency diseases

Vitamin A and night blindness

Vitamin A is necessary for normal vision, especially in dim light. Night blindness is difficulty seeing in low illumination and is a characteristic early manifestation of vitamin A deficiency. Severe or prolonged deficiency can cause further eye damage. However, night blindness may also have other causes, so the symptom alone does not establish a vitamin deficiency.

Vitamin B1 and beriberi

Vitamin B1, also called thiamine, helps the body use energy from food and supports nerve function. Severe deficiency causes beriberi, which can affect nerves and muscles and may also affect the heart. A diet dominated by highly polished cereals with little variety increases the risk of inadequate thiamine intake.

Vitamin B3 and pellagra

Severe niacin deficiency causes pellagra. Its classical features are often remembered as dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, with death possible in advanced untreated disease. The characteristic skin changes are especially noticeable on sun-exposed areas.

Vitamin C and scurvy

Vitamin C is needed to form collagen, an important component of connective tissues. Deficiency causes scurvy, with features such as swollen or bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Amla, guava, oranges and lemons are useful dietary sources.

Vitamin D and rickets

Vitamin D helps the intestine absorb calcium and supports normal bone mineralisation. Deficiency during childhood can cause rickets, in which growing bones may become soft and develop deformities. In adults, deficient mineralisation can cause osteomalacia.

Vitamin D has an unusual feature: the body can produce it in the skin after suitable exposure to sunlight. Sunlight is therefore involved in vitamin D production, but it is not itself a food source.

Other important distinctions

Folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies can both cause megaloblastic anaemia, but vitamin B12 deficiency can additionally damage the nervous system. Vitamin E has an antioxidant role; severe dietary deficiency is uncommon in otherwise healthy people. Vitamin K is needed for normal blood clotting, and severe deficiency may cause abnormal bleeding.

Important: A deficiency disease is associated with lack of a nutrient, but a matching symptom can have other medical causes. Excessive consumption of vitamin supplements is not a substitute for a balanced diet and may be harmful, particularly with some fat-soluble vitamins.

Prelims focus

  • Vitamin A deficiency: night blindness.
  • Vitamin B1 deficiency: beriberi; vitamin B3 deficiency: pellagra.
  • Vitamin C deficiency: scurvy; vitamin D deficiency: rickets in children.
  • Vitamin B9 or B12 deficiency: possible megaloblastic anaemia.
  • Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.
  • Trap: Rickets is associated with vitamin D deficiency, while scurvy is associated with vitamin C deficiency.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 12–16; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body, printed pp. 42–46, especially Fig. 3.5; US National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements, Niacin, Vitamin B12, Folate and Vitamin K Health Professional Fact Sheets, deficiency sections, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Vitamins divide into fat-soluble A, D, E, K and water-soluble B-complex and C. Most water-soluble vitamins are not stored in large amounts; B12 is an exception.
pictures.caption: Classification of vitamins by solubility.

title: Vitamins: Functions, Sources and Deficiency Diseases

body:
Why are minerals essential?

Minerals are inorganic nutrients needed for normal body structure and function. They do not provide calories, but their absence can affect growth, blood formation, bones, nerves and other important processes.

Different minerals have different roles. Iron cannot replace iodine, and calcium cannot replace iron. A varied diet is important because no single food supplies all minerals in the required proportions.

Important minerals and their deficiency disorders

MineralMain functionCommon sourcesDeficiency effect
IronFormation of haemoglobin for oxygen transportPulses, green leafy vegetables, beans, meat and iron-fortified foodsIron-deficiency anaemia, often causing fatigue and weakness
IodineProduction of thyroid hormonesIodised salt, seafood and other foods depending on iodine contentIodine-deficiency disorders, including goitre
CalciumFormation and maintenance of bones and teeth; normal muscle and nerve functionMilk, curd, paneer, some leafy vegetables and calcium-fortified foodsPoor bone mineralisation and weakened bones when deficiency is significant

Iron and anaemia

Iron is an essential component of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. When the body lacks sufficient iron, it may not produce adequate haemoglobin. This can cause iron-deficiency anaemia, with symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, pallor and shortness of breath.

Iron from plant foods is generally absorbed less efficiently than iron from animal foods. Including vitamin C-rich foods, such as amla, guava or lemon, with plant-based meals can improve the absorption of non-haem iron.

Anaemia is not always caused by iron deficiency. Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, blood loss and other medical conditions can also cause anaemia. The terms anaemia and iron deficiency are therefore not interchangeable.

Iodine and the thyroid gland

The thyroid gland, located in the neck, requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones. These hormones help regulate metabolism and are important for growth and development.

Long-term iodine deficiency may cause enlargement of the thyroid gland, producing a swelling in the neck called goitre. Severe deficiency during pregnancy and early development can impair normal growth and brain development. Not every enlarged thyroid is caused by iodine deficiency, but iodine deficiency is a preventable cause.

Why is iodised salt important?

Iodised salt is common salt to which an iodine compound has been added in a suitable amount. This process is an example of food fortification, which means adding one or more nutrients to a food to improve its nutritional value.

Double-fortified salt contains added iodine and iron. Ordinary iodised salt should not be confused with double-fortified salt, because iodine fortification alone does not provide additional iron.

Gujarat connection: salt production and iodine

Agariya communities practise traditional salt production in the Little Rann of Kutch and other parts of Gujarat. Salt production and salt iodisation are different activities. Salt obtained from seawater does not automatically have the iodine content required of iodised salt; iodine must be supplied through an appropriate fortification process.

Calcium and vitamin D work together

Calcium is an important mineral in bones and teeth. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium from the intestine. Therefore, adequate calcium intake and sufficient vitamin D are both important for normal bone health.

Their functions are related but not identical. Calcium is a mineral used in bone structure, whereas vitamin D is a vitamin that helps regulate calcium absorption and use. This explains why deficiency of either can contribute to bone problems.

Prelims focus

  • Iron is needed for haemoglobin formation; deficiency can cause anaemia.
  • Iodine is needed for thyroid hormone production; deficiency can cause goitre.
  • Calcium is important for bones and teeth.
  • Vitamin D helps the intestine absorb calcium.
  • Iodised salt contains added iodine; double-fortified salt contains iodine and iron.
  • Trap: The presence of goitre does not prove that iodine deficiency is its only possible cause.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 13–16; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body, printed pp. 42–46, including Fig. 3.5 and the account of Agariya salt production on p. 43; ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, Guideline 1; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, Fortified Food guidance, consulted 3 November 2026.]
